These inherited ideas cannot simply be treated as products of the material conditions that exist in the new generation’s own present. They came from the past.
But once they enter new conditions, they begin to change.

Put another way, no genuinely new idea or way of looking at the world can develop without inheriting older intellectual material and transforming it in a new way to match changes in material conditions.

This is the spirit behind Lenin’s discussion of the three sources of Marxism. He argued that Marxism did not arise outside the main course of human intellectual development. On the contrary, it answered questions that humanity had already been asking throughout earlier ages.
This idea also expresses the Marxist position toward national and global cultural heritage.
The aim is to preserve that heritage, but not simply because it is heritage.

The aim is to discover within it those elements of human thought that are shared across different peoples and generations, and then to follow those elements through their continuing development and change.
This development takes place through a double process: first, changes in society; and second, the changes in human consciousness that necessarily follow from them.

Seen in this light, we can clearly see how empty the attempts are of certain sections of the Arab intelligentsia who call for the Arab cultural heritage to be discarded, or for all engagement with it to end.
This nihilist position is the direct opposite of the Salafi call to “modernize” the heritage in the sense discussed earlier.
The Salafi position treats past and present as if they were essentially the same. The nihilist position treats them as complete opposites.

The first wants to make the present subordinate to the past. In doing so, it alienates modern Arab society and modern Arab thought from their own age and from the revolutionary changes taking place within it.

The second wants to cut the present off from the past. In doing so, it alienates modern Arab society and modern Arab thought from their own history and from the roots that confirm their genuine place within that history.
So although these two positions appear to be opposites, they meet on common ground.
Both uproot Arab society and Arab thought from the present itself.
One uproots them from historical authenticity. The other uproots them from modern life.

Both are therefore forms of separation from the present, because the present exists through a dialectical unity between historical roots and contemporary life. It is the unity of the relationship between past, present, and future.
Once one side of this unity is torn away, the unity itself loses its meaning. The present can no longer remain fully present in the historical and dialectical sense.

This is why the call to abandon all engagement with the heritage—whatever its ideological starting point—rests on assumptions that are rejected by the actual logic of social and historical reality. And in questions of this kind, that reality is the final test of whether an idea, theory, or assumption is sound.

After these methodological explanations, we can now move to a critical historical survey of the different positions taken toward the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage in general, and toward its philosophical part in particular, both in the past and in the present.
This survey is itself methodologically necessary.

It will allow us to compare these different positions with the theoretical and ideological principles we have already set out. We can then see where they agree with those principles and where they depart from them, and we can ask what lies behind each agreement or disagreement.

In the end, this should also allow us to give a brief answer, here in the introduction, to a question that has been with us since the idea for this book first arose and remained with us throughout the years of research that produced it:

Why do we need another work on the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage, and especially its philosophical heritage, after so much has already been written about it from the end of the Middle Ages to the second half of the twentieth century?
Our survey of the different positions taken toward this heritage—across both older and modern works—showed us how to answer that question.

We found that many of these positions, despite the very different periods they came from, the different societies in which they appeared, and the different bodies of knowledge and standards they used to judge the heritage, remained fundamentally one-sided.

We mentioned this at the beginning of the introduction. We now need to examine the matter in much greater detail and show why we believe that one-sidedness dominates the overwhelming majority of these positions.
This will not be a simple list of authors and books.

That kind of approach is very far from our method, because it comes too close to a purely subjective treatment. Still, some listing may occasionally be unavoidable while we analyze the different positions and group them into broader currents.
The people who have written histories, interpretations, and studies of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage come from very different backgrounds.
They belong to different periods, societies, and ideological traditions. They come from different countries, and the knowledge they bring to the heritage also varies greatly.

Some are ancient, others modern. Some are progressive, others conservative. Some are materialists, others idealists. Some are Salafis, others nihilists. Some are Arab, some Eastern, and some Western. Among them are historians, theologians, social researchers, and philosophers.
These identities overlap in complicated ways. We therefore cannot use a simple classification that separates each one from the others.
We need a classification that reflects the overlap itself.
For this reason, we will use two different but overlapping forms of classification.
The first is methodological. It is based on the different ways scholars have viewed the heritage and the different intellectual methods they have used to deal with it.
The second is descriptive. It divides researchers into three broad groups:
Ancient Arab and Eastern writers, from the Middle Ages through the later period up to the eighteenth century.
Modern Arab and Eastern writers, from the nineteenth century to our own time in the twentieth century.
Other researchers from different national backgrounds, especially Orientalists.
The first, methodological classification cuts across all three groups in the second classification.
Every researcher within those groups can be placed, broadly speaking, within one of the following four intellectual approaches.
First: treating the history of thought as a history of ideas alone
The first approach treats the history of thought, especially philosophy, as nothing more than a history of ideas or the product of “personal” thought.

It connects ideas only to the individuals who produced them, without asking how either those ideas or those individuals were related to the conditions of their age or to the society in which they lived and thought.
It therefore ignores the historical character of social relations and ignores the interaction between intellectual life and the economic, social, political, and historical relationships around it.

Those who have used this method to discuss the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage—across all three groups in our descriptive classification—have usually done little more than present a chronological account of the names and ideas of Arab-Islamic thinkers and philosophers.
Their explanations remain detached from the interaction between those thinkers and the societies and periods in which they lived.
There is, however, one kind of relationship to which these historians and researchers often pay close attention: the influence of one thinker on another.
They look at the influence of earlier thinkers on later ones, or at the influence of thinkers outside the Arab-Islamic tradition—Greek, Persian, or Indian—on individual Arab-Islamic thinkers.
In other words, they reduce historical relationships to relationships between individuals and to personal intellectual influence.

It is as if every thinker existed in a world of his own, separate from social reality, and as if intellectual influence passed directly between these isolated worlds without being shaped by social relations.
This way of thinking is clearly idealist.
Second: treating cultural influence as a simple mechanical transfer
The second approach sees the exchange between cultures in purely mechanical terms.

It assumes that once the culture of one people reaches another people, by whatever means, it can simply take control of their thinking, erase the distinctive features of their own culture, and replace them with the characteristics of the incoming culture.
Many studies of Arab-Islamic philosophy have taken this view.

This is especially true of some European Orientalists who claimed that Arab-Islamic philosophy was Arab or Islamic only in the sense that it was an Arabic copy of Greek philosophy, which the Arabs and Muslims simply adopted in its various “Pythagorean,” Platonic, Aristotelian, and Neoplatonic forms.
Some modern Arab researchers followed a similar approach.

One of them, for example, claimed that the Islamic spirit had been unable to understand the spirit of Greek philosophy, and that none of the Muslims who studied Greek philosophy possessed a genuinely philosophical spirit. Otherwise, he argued, they would have absorbed Greek philosophy fully, moved on to real intellectual creation, and produced a new philosophy of their own.
There is an obvious difference between these two claims.
The first gives the philosophical work of the Arabs and Muslims a purely Greek character.
The second goes further and denies it even that much, because it denies that Arab-Islamic thinkers possessed a true philosophical spirit at all.
But despite this difference, both claims rest on the same simplified, mechanical way of thinking about the relationship between the thought of one people and the thought of another.

The first sees only the external form of the questions discussed by Arab-Islamic philosophy. It fails to understand that this form belonged to philosophy more generally during the historical period extending into the Middle Ages.

The second assumes that the only proof of a true philosophical spirit would have been for Arab-Islamic philosophers to discuss exactly the same questions as Greek philosophy. When it does not find those same questions reproduced in exactly the same way, it denies that Arab-Islamic thought was philosophical at all.
But the relationship between two intellectual or philosophical traditions belonging to two different societies is much more complicated than this.
It is part of the relationship between internal and external forms of social consciousness, and that relationship follows its own laws and its own dialectical movement.
The first basic feature of these laws is that they are objective. They do not depend simply on individual choice or intention.
The second is that ideas coming from outside can only become active and influential within a society by passing through its own internal relationships.

In other words, outside ideas can only become effective through the questions that already form part of the social fabric of that society—questions shaped by its own circumstances, its material relations of production, and its particular history.

Because these researchers did not approach Arab-Islamic philosophy in this way, they were unable to understand the inner dialectic of Arab thought in general, and Arab philosophical thought in particular.
They failed, first, to understand its relationship with Islam as thought, belief, and social system.

Second, they failed to understand its relationship with the questions facing Arab-Islamic society itself. These questions formed an extremely complicated web in which social and political issues were intertwined with religious, doctrinal, and legal ones.

And because they failed to understand this, they were also unable to understand the relationship between what was purely internal to Arab thought and what came from outside, whether through Greek thought in the West or Persian and Indian thought in the East.
This simplified mechanical view allowed them to deny the philosophical originality of Arab-Islamic thought.
Had they understood both sides of the problem—the inner logic of Arab thought and the way it interacted with thought coming from outside—they would have seen the heart of the matter more easily.

Greek philosophy could only have had its well-known historical influence on Arab-Islamic philosophy by being absorbed, transformed, and reshaped through the internal workings of Arab-Islamic thought itself.
Through this process, Greek philosophy became part of an Arab-Islamic reality and acquired a new life that was different from its purely Greek form.
Third: explaining cultural differences in racial terms
The third approach explains differences between national cultures through race.
This is the worst of the approaches we are discussing.
It is not only a form of idealist thinking. It also grows out of a colonial and fascist ideology that places peoples in a hierarchy based on a “theory of race” that science rejected long ago.
A number of researchers have approached the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage in this racial way. They include Orientalists, Arabs, and other Eastern writers.
Some still approach it in this spirit today, consciously in some cases and unconsciously in others.
The fourth approach is to study the heritage historically.

The people who use this approach differ greatly in their methods, but they share one basic principle: they look for the relationship between inherited intellectual works and the historical conditions in which those works were produced.
Their differences come from the different ways they understand this relationship and from how deeply they trace it.
Some deal only with secondary or surface-level historical connections. Others try to reach the more fundamental ones.
